title: Autoscaler request-weighting blindspot causing reserved-pool burst shortfalls
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
Customers on Dedicated pools observed unexplained capacity shortfalls during sustained mixed workloads. Investigation shows the autoscaler aggregation signal weights requests by QPS (per-request count) rather than token cost or weighted concurrency. In multi-tenant pools with many short-lived, high-token requests (batch embeddings, long prompts with streaming), the current metric underestimates true GPU load and the reserved pool does not provision burst capacity in time, exhausting burst limits and triggering throttling/fallback routing.

Reproduction steps observed in prod: 
- Tenant A issues many short requests (QPS spike) with small token footprint -> autoscaler responds normally.
- Tenant B issues fewer concurrent requests but each consumes long output sequences (high token throughput). Because autoscaler signal uses request count, high-token requests are effectively down-weighted, so headroom calculations and burst accounting do not reflect real token throughput.
- Result: pool hits GPU compute saturation while autoscaler still believes headroom exists, leading to request queuing, increased latency, and reserve-burst exhaustion for affected tenants.

Root cause hypothesis: 
1) Autoscaler metric pipeline uses a RequestCountTimeseries aggregated with exponential smoothing; token-based metrics exist but are sampled at a lower frequency and not included in the scale policy.
2) Burst-credit accounting and eager allocation use the same aggregated signal; when token throughput surges briefly, the eager allocation path is not triggered due to QPS-focused heuristics.
3) Multi-tenant headroom fragmentation: small tenants leave unusable fractional GPU capacity that cannot be reallocated quickly for a tenant with sudden token-heavy requests.

Why this is unique/different from prior incidents: 
- Past incidents focused on headroom miscalculation or oscillation during long-lived load patterns. This ticket isolates a weighting/feature-flag gap where the autoscaler is blind to token-cost density per request, causing under-provisioning for token-heavy bursts even when QPS is low.

Work to do (high level):
- Short-term mitigation (hotfix): add a token-rate derived signal into the autoscaler aggregate used for burst-trigger thresholds; increase sampling frequency for token counters for Dedicated pools. Backfill for last 72h and run in Canary.
- Mid-term: refactor scale policy to support composite signals: request-count, token-rate, and avg-latency-weighted-concurrency with configurable weights per-pool. Add tenant-weighted allocation logic to avoid headroom fragmentation.
- Long-term: evaluate fine-grained per-tenant scheduling (soft reservations) so burst credits can be atomically allocated across fractional capacity.

Immediate customer actions: 
- Notified three impacted customers (ACME Health, BentoSearch, QueryFlow) with timeline and mitigation steps. Provided temporary quota increase and manual reserved pool top-up while hotfix is validated.
- Ops to monitor rollback triggers and be ready to revert if jitter or overscale occurs.

Artifacts and links: 
- Incident timeline and metrics dashboard: https://console.redwood/team/dedicated/autoscale-incident-2026-02
- Investigation notes (Confluence): https://confluence.redwoodinternal.com/display/ENG/ENG-55678+investigation
- Hotfix PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821
- Telemetry query used for reproduction: https://telemetry.redwood/q/queries/autoscale-token-weighting

Acceptance criteria for this ticket: 
- Hotfix deployed to canary pool for 48h with no regression (latency, cost) and accurate token-rate signal reflected in scale decisions.
- At least two CI-driven replay tests that simulate mixed workloads (short/long requests) show autoscaler triggers within SLOs without excessive overscale.
- Postmortem updates with action items and updated runbook for Reserved Pool burst accounting.

Notes on risk and roll-forward strategy: 
- Adding token-rate into scale signal increases sensitivity; must tune smoothing window to avoid oscillation.
- If hotfix causes overscaling (cost spike), we will revert and iterate with a conservative weight.
